newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Buba's Zeitler tough but upbeat on EMU hopes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Buba's Zeitler tough but upbeat on EMU hopes.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler on Tuesday expressed confidence that Germany could meet Maastricht goals and 2.5 percent growth this year, but warned that EMU targets should not be softened.

"Nothing is absolutely certain," Zeitler told a news conference when asked about prospects for a timely euro launch amid doubts that Germany can overcome massive unemployment to meet the tough Maastricht budgetary convergence criteria.
"But whoever sets a goal also means to meet that goal. And I see good and realistic chances to meet the deficit criterion for monetary union," Zeitler said.

Zeitler also welcomed France's decision to hold early elections as a sign of commitment to Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), but stressed again that sustainable fulfilment of Maastricht criteria took precedence over the January 1999 deadline for the start of the euro project.

While shying from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer's unusually candid message on Monday that the euro launch could be delayed if large countries failed to make the grade, Zeitler said there should be no talk of softening EMU goals.
"The foundation of a house is more important than the moving-in date," he said.

Alongside a range of targets for inflation and exchange rates, the Maastricht Treaty calls on countries to cut their budget deficits to no more than three percent of gross domestic product and their state debt levels to no more than 60 percent of GDP in order to take part in EMU.

Zeitler noted that Germany's top six economic institutes had on Tuesday projected a German budget deficit ratio of 3.0 to 3.2 percent this year -- a decisive threshold for the choice of countries to launch the euro.
That forecast confirmed his optimism, Zeitler said, as did the institutes' forecast for 2.25 percent growth in Germany this year.
This is in line with his own growth expectations, based partly on a better outlook for export business on the back of the weaker deutschemark.
But there was no further need for the mark to correct further from its strong levels of 1995, he added.

Turning to the German economic outlook in detail, Zeitler also said that at present he saw no real inflation risks in Germany as growth was modest, wage deals moderate and raw materials prices were having a dampening effect.

"Overall I see no reason for a change in interest rates on the basis of fundamentals," he said, while adding that a recent rise in import prices and continued buoyant growth in M3 money supply did not auger for further rate easing.
Headline German interest rates have been held at historic lows since last August, with the floor discount rate at 2.5 percent and the money market, or repo rate, at three percent.
Keeping rates on hold did not however "exclude the possibility of temporary phases of correction on the capital market -- as happened in the previous year," he warned.

Zeitler also said it remained to be seen whether the March slowdown in the Bundesbank's key price indicator, M3 money supply growth, to an annualised rate of 8.3 percent from 9.1 percent signalled a "trend change" towards the target range of 3.5 percent to 6.5 percent.
At the same time, he said he was "confident" the goal could be reached this year.
His comments come as economists began to speculate that the Bundesbank was loosening its once unswerving allegiance to M3 as a policy guide to take other factors into account.

Zeitler noted that M3 figures had to be viewed against the background of a weakening of monetary capital formation and of the growth of extended M3 -- a measure which comprises money market funds and foreign deposits -- which has expanded more slowly than M3, rising by 2.5 percentage points in 1996.
"With this necessary analysis and supplementation the M3 figures for the year 1996 lose drama. But they remain a factor."
